# Datasets

The column that matters most is **per subject**: it is the budget every decoder
is actually spending, and it is the column most comparison tables omit.

## Caveats

Each of these will silently change a number by more than most methods claim to gain.

**Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD)**
- Papers differ on whether they average the 3 repeats of each test image. Averaging lifts every metric.
- Only 4 of 8 subjects completed all sessions, so "averaged over subjects" means different things in different papers.

**BOLD5000**
- Far fewer repeats per image than NSD; single-trial numbers here are not comparable to NSD numbers.

**Generic Object Decoding (GOD, Kamitani lab)**
- Test categories are disjoint from training categories, so this measures category generalisation. NSD does not.

**THINGS-fMRI (THINGS-data)**
- Shares its stimulus set with THINGS-MEG and THINGS-EEG, the only clean route to cross-modality comparison.

**THINGS-EEG2 (Gifford et al.)**
- RSVP means about 100 ms per image. Reconstruction quality here is bounded by the paradigm, not only by the model.

**EEG-ImageNet (Spampinato et al., CVPR 2017)**
- BLOCK DESIGN CONFOUND. All images of a class were shown in one contiguous block, so slow drift alone identifies the class. Accuracies on this dataset do not measure visual decoding. See docs/pitfalls.md. Do not use for new work.

**Natural language fMRI dataset (LeBel et al., Moth Radio Hour)**
- This is the dataset behind Tang et al. 2023. Only a few subjects have the deep sessions the headline results rely on.

**ZuCo 1.0 / 2.0**
- Word-level EEG segments are cut using eye-tracking fixations, so any EEG-to-text result on ZuCo has eye-tracking-derived word boundaries baked into its input.
- Most published EEG-to-text numbers on ZuCo were produced with teacher forcing at evaluation time. See docs/pitfalls.md.

**Armeni et al. 10-hour MEG audiobook**
- Deepest per-subject language MEG data available, the natural target for subject-specific scaling experiments.
